Empirical Research Plan

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Utility‐border difference-in-differences (DID) / event-study combined with an instrumental-variables (IV) first stage.  
Rationale:  
a. The six Orange County cities are internally split by an administratively fixed service-territory border that is orthogonal to household characteristics.  
b. SCE and SDG&E changed their nonlinear tariffs at different moments and by different amounts from 1999-2007, generating plausibly exogenous within-city, across-time price-schedule variation.  
c. Because the marginal price facing a household is mechanically increasing in own kWh, price is endogenous. We therefore instrument household-level marginal, expected-marginal, or average price with the posted tariff parameters that differ by utility × month but are common to all households served by that utility in that month.  
d. The DID estimator with household and month-of-year × city fixed effects nets out time-invariant unobservables and common shocks, while the IV step purges simultaneity bias.

Formally:

First stage:  
P_iu,t  = π₀ + π₁·Tariff_u,t + HH_FE_i + CityMonth_FE_c,m + ε_i,t  

Second stage:

log(kWh_i,t) = β ·  P̂_iu,t  + HH_FE_i + CityMonth_FE_c,m + η_i,t  

where P is one of three alternative price concepts (marginal, expected marginal, or average).

The coefficients β across the three specifications reveal which price concept households actually respond to.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: The exogenous component of a household’s price concept, instrumented by Tariff_u,t – a vector containing the utility’s tier cut-points and per-kWh prices in each tier in month t.  
Control group: Households served by the other utility during the same month and residing in the same city.  
Treatment timing: Months in which one utility changes its tariff while the other does not (or changes by a different amount). Key events:  
• 07/2000–05/2001 SDG&E crisis spike  
• 05/2001 five-tier introduction (both utilities but with different magnitudes)  
• Numerous smaller schedule revisions 1999-2007  
No running variable / cutoff, so RDD is not used.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: Absent tariff changes, kWh for households on each side of the border would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Strong—the cities share climate, economic trends, and natural-gas provider; we include city-by-month-of-year FE and test for pre-treatment trend equality in an event-study.  

A2. Exogeneity of tariff changes to individual demand shocks: Utility-level schedule revisions are driven by regulation, legacy cost recovery, and generation portfolios, not by contemporaneous consumption of specific border households.  
Plausibility: High—CPUC sets tariffs at the utility level; households cannot choose utility.  

A3. No cross-border spillovers: Consumption of a treated household does not directly affect the control household’s price schedule and vice-versa.  
Plausibility: Very high; tariffs are set for the entire utility, not city-specific.  

A4. Stable composition: Sample restricted to stayers eliminates selective migration in response to price.  
Plausibility: Reasonable; address changes drop out.  

A5. First-stage relevance: Utility × month tariff variation moves the instrumented price concepts.  
Plausibility: Guaranteed by construction and documented in tariff filings.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
T1. Differential non-price utility policies (rebates, outage shocks).  
Fix: Collect utility program/outage data; include utility-specific linear trends and utility × weather interactions; drop months with rolling blackouts.  

T2. Remaining demographic differences within split cities.  
Fix: Add Census block-group controls interacted with flexible time trends; re-estimate on households ≤1 km from border (“geo-matched” subsample).  

T3. Measurement error in expected marginal price (requires predicted future tier placement).  
Fix: Define expected marginal price using a 12-month moving average of own past usage; show robustness to alternative forecasting windows; employ classical-error IV correction by using utility-level schedule changes only.

5. R Code Outline
```r
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(lubridate)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
sce   <- fread("sce_billing.csv")        # same column structure
sdge  <- fread("sdge_billing.csv")
tarif <- fread("utility_tariff_schedule.csv") # utility, month, tier1, tier2, ...

# Combine utilities -------------------------------------------------------
sce[, utility := "SCE"]
sdge[, utility := "SDGE"]
dt <- rbindlist(list(sce, sdge), use.names = TRUE)

# Keep analytic sample ----------------------------------------------------
dt <- dt[analytic_sample == 1]           # assume flag pre-created
dt[, month_id := as.yearmon(billing_end_date)]

# 2. Merge tariff schedule ------------------------------------------------
dt <- merge(dt, tarif, by = c("utility","month_id"), all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Construct price variables -------------------------------------------
# realized marginal price = price of tier in which current kWh falls
dt[, tier := fifelse(kWh <= tier1_kWh, 1,
              fifelse(kWh <= tier2_kWh, 2,
              fifelse(kWh <= tier3_kWh, 3,
              fifelse(kWh <= tier4_kWh, 4, 5))))]
price_cols <- paste0("p_tier",1:5)
dt[, P_marg := get(price_cols)[cbind(.I, tier)] ]

# average price
dt[, P_avg := bill_amount / kWh ]

# expected marginal: use previous 12-mo mean usage to locate expected tier
setorder(dt, account_id, month_id)
dt[, kWh_lag12 := frollmean(kWh, n = 12, align = "right"), by = account_id]
dt[, exp_tier := fifelse(kWh_lag12 <= tier1_kWh,1,
                 fifelse(kWh_lag12 <= tier2_kWh,2,
                 fifelse(kWh_lag12 <= tier3_kWh,3,
                 fifelse(kWh_lag12 <= tier4_kWh,4,5))))]
dt[, P_expMarg := get(price_cols)[cbind(.I, exp_tier)] ]

# 4. Instrumental variables: utility-month posted schedule ---------------
# Here we use tariff-level mean marginal price of each tier as instrument
dt[, Z_marg := P_marg, by = .(utility, month_id)]             # identical within utility-month
dt[, Z_exp  := P_expMarg, by = .(utility, month_id)]
dt[, Z_avg  := P_avg, by = .(utility, month_id)]              # pseudo-average under uniform 1kWh

# 5. Main regression ------------------------------------------------------
# Household FE + city*month-of-year FE
dt[, city_month := interaction(city, month(billing_end_date))]

fe_formula <- " | account_id + city_month"

# (i) Marginal price response
est_marg <- feols(log(kWh) ~ 1 | account_id + city_month,
                  iv = ~ P_marg | Z_marg,
                  data = dt)
# (ii) Expected marginal price response
est_exp  <- feols(log(kWh) ~ 1 | account_id + city_month,
                  iv = ~ P_expMarg | Z_exp,
                  data = dt)
# (iii) Average price response
est_avg  <- feols(log(kWh) ~ 1 | account_id + city_month,
                  iv = ~ P_avg | Z_avg,
                  data = dt)

etable(est_marg, est_exp, est_avg, se = "cluster", cluster = ~block_group)

# 6. Robustness: geo-matched sample within 1 km of border -----------------
dt_geo <- dt[border_distance <= 1000]
est_geo <- feols(log(kWh) ~ 1 | account_id + city_month,
                 iv = ~ P_avg | Z_avg,
                 data = dt_geo)
etable(est_avg, est_geo)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory with inattentive or confused consumers suggests they overweight average price because it appears on the bill, while the marginal price is cognitively demanding. My prior:  
• Elasticity w.r.t. average price ≈ −0.20 (standard residential short-run).  
• Elasticity w.r.t. realized marginal price close to 0 (|β| < 0.05).  
• Elasticity w.r.t. expected marginal price somewhere between (≈ −0.10).  
Implication: Nonlinear prices reduce consumption less than regulators assume if they expect full marginal-price salience; welfare losses from misoptimization could thus be material.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = doubtful)  
C1: Parallel trends tested and visually confirmed …… 1  
C2: Exogeneity of utility tariff changes ………………… 1  
C3: No within-city spillovers / interference ………… 1  
C4: No differential compositional change …………… 0.5 (migration limited but not nil)  
C5: Strong first-stage relevance ………………………… 1  

Total: 4.5 / 5
